study.title: Psalm 114 The presence of the Lord that shakes creation and supply the people
study.overview: Psalm 114 celebrates, in poetic and vibrant language, the departure of Israel from Egypt and the mighty acts of God in the history of his people. The psalm unites memory, worship and reverence: the exodus, the crossing of the sea, the passage of the Jordan, the tremor of the mountains, and finally the miracle of the water that springs from the rock. The emphasis is not only on recalling ancient events, but in recognizing that the presence of the God of Jacob dominates creation and helps his people in difficult times.

outline.title: The exit of Egypt and the people as a place of God's presence
outline.explanation: The psalm begins by remembering the deliverance of Jacob's house from a foreign people. Judah is called the sanctuary of God and Israel of their dominions, showing that the identity of the people was formed by the divine action and by the presence of the Lord among them.

outline.title: Creation reacts to the Lord's march
outline.explanation: The sea flees, the Jordan retreats, and mountains and hills are described as if they leaped before the divine presence. Language embodies nature to highlight that the most stable elements of creation move when God acts for his people.

outline.title: Reverence before the God of Jacob providing water
outline.explanation: The whole earth is called to tremble before the Lord. The psalm ends by remembering that he turned rock into a lake and boulder into a fountain, uniting power and provision in a single image of miraculous care.

study.context: The notes connect the psalm to the exodus, to the crossing of the sea and to the passage of the Jordan, and also to the provision of water in the desert. There is an indication that the separate mention of Judah and Israel suggests composition after the division of the kingdom, and perhaps after exile. This, however, is an interpretative inference of the notes, not a date explicitly affirmed by the biblical text.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that the redemption of Israel was not mere political ransom, but a revealing act of God, who formed a people for themselves and established in him his presence. The creation answers to the voice of the Lord: water go back, mountains tremble, the earth trembles. This shows God's sovereign government of nature and history. At the same time, the same God who frightens creation also cares for his people, turning stone into water. Thus, power and mercy do not appear separate: the Lord who judges the pride of the world is the same that sustains its with concrete provision.

scholarViews.insight: The Psalm is a lyrical celebration of the Lord's power in nature, linked to the exodus and entry into the promised land, and culminates in reverence to the God of Jacob.
The liberation of Egypt is presented as the birth of the church and the nation of Israel, a work of wonder that should not be forgotten.
The mention of Judah as a sanctuary and Israel as dominion suggests that the psalm was written after the division of the tribes, when that distinction already existed.

questions: What does it mean, in practice, to remember the ancient works of God without treating memory as something only emotional?
In what ways does creation in this psalm reveal God's authority over all that seems fixed and unshakable?
How does the image of God turning rock into a fountain corrects expectations of provision in difficult times?
study.practice: Practice a devotional reading that unites memory and reverence: remember a concrete deliverance that God has already granted, thank him and ask that this memory produces trust in the present. It is also worth observing whether his vision of God is limited to abstract spiritual blessings, when the psalm shows a Lord who acts in history and supplies real needs. In prayer, recognize your sovereignty over circumstances that seem harsh as a stone.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not inform date, authorship or precise historical circumstances; the idea of composition after the division of the kingdom or after exile comes from the notes and should be treated as inference, not as certainty. There is also a difference in emphasis between the commentators: some see the psalm mainly as the celebration of the exodus, while others more strongly highlight the possible subsequent composition.
